definition: Unilateral means done by one side alone, without the agreement or consent of the others involved — one-sided action where cooperation was expected.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word unilateral. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know unilateral should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Employees were stunned by the CEO's unilateral decision to cancel the remote-work policy overnight.
An independent choice is simply made on your own; a unilateral one is made alone when others expected a say.
A unilateral decision skips the group once, but a dictatorial leader silences the group every single time.

One-sided describes a thing that is unbalanced in favor of one side — a one-sided contest, a one-sided account. Unilateral is about the acting, not the imbalance: one party moves alone, without the agreement of the others who expected a say.

Solo means done by one person alone, and it is neutral or even admiring — a solo flight, a solo album. Unilateral carries a sting solo lacks: the decision affected other parties who were entitled to be consulted and never were.

High-handed describes the overbearing manner of someone using power without regard for others — bossy, dismissive, presuming. Unilateral is narrower and more technical: it states the structural fact that one side acted without the others' consent, whatever the tone.

Unilateral means done by one side alone, without the agreement or consent of the others involved — one-sided action where cooperation was expected.
Without checking with his roommates, Theo made the unilateral choice to repaint their shared kitchen bright orange while they were away for the weekend.
The kitchen belongs to everyone, so everyone expected a say — but Theo acted entirely on his own.
Unilateral flags a one-sided action taken where agreement was expected.
Formal — political, often critical

Unilateral is this unit's deliberate odd one out: while most Unit 11 words describe sides coming together, unilateral describes one side acting alone, without the consent of the others involved — and it often carries a critical edge ('a unilateral decision' hints that others should have been consulted).
Its natural opposites are the unit's own cooperation words: mutual and reciprocal describe exactly what unilateral actions lack, and multilateral describes many parties acting together.

For twenty years the four observatories shared the mountaintop telescope under a schedule hammered out each January by all four directors.
This winter, the largest observatory simply published next year's calendar on its own, assigning itself the moonless nights and scattering the rest.
Its director saw no scandal.
The paperwork was flawless, the tone of the covering letter warm, and her observatory had, after all, paid for the new mirror.
The other three called the move unilateral, and the word carried the charge that mattered: not that the schedule was unfair, but that a decision all four were entitled to make had been made by one.
By spring, two of the three were drafting plans for a telescope of their own.
